# Running the Design Loop {#sec-running-the-loop}

::: {.epigraph}
> *"Beware of bugs in the above code; I have only proved it correct, not tried it."*
>
> — Donald E. Knuth, *Notes on the van Emde Boas Construction of Priority Deques* (1977) [@Knuth1977PriorityDeques]
:::

::: {.column-margin}
**Author's Note.** Just as Donald E. Knuth famously separated abstract reasoning about code from the hard evidence of running it, we must bring the exact same discipline to our architectural studies. A well-defined comparison, a plausible teaching fixture, or a meticulously reasoned plan does not suddenly transform into execution evidence until we actually run our tools and rigorously retain the resulting artifacts. Consequently, the prospective cache record and the executed array record we present in this chapter lead us to entirely different conclusions.
:::

::: {.callout-crux}
What hard conclusions can we draw as architects when our prospective Lighthouse cache study fails to run, and what distinct insights can our separate, fully executed array study firmly establish?
:::

We drive architectural research questions through a rigorous loop of candidate selection, execution, measurement, and decision-making. We present two distinct records that reach different stopping points. We isolate them to highlight distinct phases of our methodology, avoiding an artificial end-to-end narrative.

Our first record, the Lighthouse cache study, distills a broad 3\ W RISC-V system objective into a single pre-RTL decision on L2 capacity. We treat this record as strictly prospective, mapping out required comparisons while exposing the uncompleted engineering effort blocking simulation. It never executes, leaving baseline and candidates unresolved. In contrast, our second record is a fully realized [retained systolic-array study](https://github.com/harvard-edge/arch2/tree/f5516e52e66243c2d753191e350a5cfac56c83af/labs/examples/ai_systolic_array_study) using SCALE-Sim. Across twelve simulator evaluation events, it demonstrates the insights unlocked by real execution. However, because it evaluates isolated GEMM layers rather than full subsystem pipelines, it cannot patch our cache gaps or validate our 3\ W target.

::: {.callout-learning-objectives}
After reading this chapter, we can

- Navigate an architectural research question from fixed state to a rigorous stopping decision.
- Distinguish prospective experimental plans from executed empirical evidence.
- Isolate the architectural outcome, AI contribution, mechanism result, and actionable next steps.
- Leverage ties, failed causal explanations, and provenance gaps to properly scope follow-up studies.
:::

## Prospective Cache Design Study

We must first define our target architecture decision. Until we clearly establish the candidate configurations, controlled design parameters, functional checks, and permitted conclusions, our executable tool path lacks a rigorous baseline comparison. We then need to identify exactly what infrastructure must exist to run that comparison. Formally declaring these requirements exposes our remaining engineering work without inadvertently fabricating a preliminary cache result.

### Architectural Decision

We begin our Lighthouse cache study by focusing on a concrete architectural decision across the 8 layers of our prompt stack rather than reaching for an AI method. Our overarching system goal targets the 3\ W TDP XR compute subsystem introduced in @sec-moonshot, mapped to a TSMC N7 or 3\ nm-class LP mobile process. Here, we ask a fundamental design question about which, if either, of two larger L2 capacities should advance to RTL evaluation against our current baseline. To ensure that our capacity change is the sole cause of any measured performance difference, we strictly hold the rest of our RV64GCV ISA contract, vector-capable CPU and NPU accelerator compute organization, XRBench (an extended reality benchmark suite) / SPEC2026 (a CPU benchmark suite) / MLPerf (a machine learning benchmark suite) workload snapshot, Triton (a domain-specific compiler framework) JIT to RVV 1.0 compiler stack, and planned tool path fixed.

Our comparison explicitly tests a 2\ MiB baseline against 3\ MiB and 4\ MiB candidates. These capacities define the distinct architectural objects within our prospective study. We should note that they are not yet fully fleshed-out cache configurations, generated RTL instances, or measured artifacts stored in our repository.

While capacity serves as our only swept architecture parameter (limited to the 2, 3, and 4\ MiB choices), this does not imply that every underlying hardware request remains identical. A larger cache capacity naturally demands a different set count, bank organization, or SRAM macro composition. Before we dispatch any simulation jobs, we must establish a rigorous rule that derives these dependent structural values. At the same time, this rule must hold our core microarchitectural features constant, including associativity, line size, indexing scheme, replacement policy, miss status holding register (MSHR) count, port configurations, hit-latency allocation, and our process, voltage, and temperature (PVT) assumptions. Because our repository currently lacks both this structural derivation rule and the explicitly bound values for our controlled cache and PVT parameters, we cannot yet execute the comparison.

Our fixed architectural state extends far beyond the cache itself. It encompasses the network-on-chip and memory-system configurations (modeling SRAM traffic in SCALE-Sim and LPDDR5X DRAM timing in Ramulator, a cycle-accurate DRAM simulator), our 2\ GHz host RV64GCV vector-capable CPU microarchitecture, the Triton JIT compiler and runtime lowering environment, the RISC-V software image, and an XRBench workload snapshot featuring perfectly stable frame identifiers and boundaries. We plan a tool path that integrates gem5, a cycle-accurate full-system simulator, for host RV64GCV cores, CACTI, an analytical memory area and access-time model, for SRAM macro access latencies, McPAT, a power and area modeling framework, for 3\ W TDP envelope estimation, IEEE 1801 UPF power domain checks, Cadence Jasper, a formal property verification environment, for formal SVA / BMC verification, and Ansys RedHawk-SC, a thermal signoff tool, for thermal signoff. However, we have not yet formally bound these conceptual tool roles to executable scripts or retained measurement pipelines in our repository.

At its core, our architecture claim asserts that a larger L2 cache will reduce 99th-percentile frame times by eliminating capacity misses, all while satisfying our strict power, area, access-time, functional correctness, and coherence constraints. We cannot validate this claim simply by showing a reduction in miss rates. Instead, our matched frame observations must prove that resolving these capacity misses directly improves our tail-latency outcomes under the rigidly fixed workload and software conditions.

Because our legal design space contains only the baseline and two discrete alternatives, our study relies on direct evaluation, as discussed in @sec-methods-generation-prediction-optimization. We intentionally avoid introducing any complex generators, predictors, optimizers, or learned search methodologies. Furthermore, our SRAM model acts strictly as a component of the declared tool path rather than as a newly integrated AI module. Omitting these advanced methods ensures our cache study carries no extraneous AI-contribution claims to test. Instead, direct evaluation provides the most streamlined approach capable of answering our targeted architecture question, assuming our tool path is fully operational.

Ultimately, we expect a highly focused result. Our study can, at most, recommend a single cache capacity to advance toward rigorous RTL evaluation. It inherently cannot authorize a full implementation, final signoff, tapeout, or any binding product commitment. We deliberately leave broader architectural explorations (such as cache replacement policies, prefetching mechanisms, floorplanning, and thermal signoffs) outside the scope of this study.

### Execution Prerequisites

Before we can execute any candidate configuration, we must systematically translate each cache capacity into a tightly controlled evaluation request, bind an executable path capable of returning both empirical measurements and failure states, and explicitly declare our stopping conditions and advancement criteria. We logically group this preparatory work into candidate definition, executable path and returns, and stopping and decision parameters. Together, these categories clearly delineate the candidates, fixed hardware states, functional checks, computational budgets, and specific tool responsibilities that we must lock down prior to execution. We emphasize that none of these declarations constitutes an actually executed request (@tbl-cache-run-declaration).

| **Run parameter** | **Declared Lighthouse cache study work** |
| --- | --- |
| **Candidate requests** | We must prepare one complete request to the SRAM model under our declared PVT conditions for the 2\ MiB baseline, 3\ MiB candidate, and 4\ MiB candidate. We will treat `l2.capacity` as the sole swept architecture parameter while strictly holding associativity, line size, indexing, replacement, MSHR count, ports, hit-latency allocation, and PVT fixed. A prospectively bound rule must derive set count, bank count, layout geometry, modeled periphery, and SRAM macro composition directly from this capacity. We will retain every controlled and derived value alongside our SRAM-model and underlying technology identities. Because our repository currently lacks these explicit bindings, our requests remain unfinished. |
| **Cycle-level requests** | We must rerun the 2\ MiB baseline alongside our eligible candidates through our cycle-level simulator. This execution includes our cache and power models while holding the declared XR workload snapshot, the software image, and all other hardware and software identities strictly fixed. |
| **Dispatch condition** | We consider no request eligible until we fully bind the controlled policy parameters alongside all capacity-derived set, bank, geometry, periphery, and macro choices. Furthermore, a cycle-level request becomes eligible for execution only when `(return_complete == true) && (schema_valid == true) && (area_mm2 <= 1.5) && (access_time_ns <= 2.5)`. We use this condition strictly to authorize a simulation request; it does not independently validate a measurement or definitively reject an architecture candidate. |
| **Required returns** | We must retain SRAM area, access time, cache-local dynamic energy, leakage, matched frame records, frame-time inputs, and the critical 99th-percentile frame time. We also require a detailed breakdown of cache misses by classification, overall subsystem dynamic and leakage power, tool versions, model identities, translated inputs, warnings, failures, cryptographic hashes, data lineage, and precise accounting records covering queue wait times, run times, compute resource use, license checkout, storage footprints, and human setup time. However, we have not yet defined the operational procedure that will generate these cost records. |
| **Checks** | We require identical ISA-visible outputs across our declared tests and mandate the same rigorous functional regression suite for every evaluated capacity. We demand zero failures from the simulator's built-in coherence-invariant checks, modeled subsystem power (dynamic plus leakage) capped at 3\ W, total cache macro area at or below 1.5\ mm^2^, and a modeled access time not exceeding 2.5\ ns. Ultimately, we require an uncertainty-qualified frame-time comparison against our rerun baseline. We treat detailed thermal and IR-drop signoff as independent requirements reserved for later design stages. |
| **Failure handling** | We will actively refuse any invalid evaluation request prior to simulation invocation. When failures occur, we must cleanly distinguish among timeouts, job cancellations, underlying infrastructure failures, stale state corruption, missing outputs, and parser errors. If we authorize a retry, we must meticulously link it to its parent attempt, deduct it from our cycle-level budget, and launch it from a freshly generated clean state without altering the underlying architecture candidate. |
| **Budget** | We permit three total SRAM model evaluations and restrict our cycle-level executions to a maximum of four, explicitly accounting for any infrastructure-driven reruns. We do not include any RTL synthesis or physical signoff in this exploratory budget. Before executing the study, we must explicitly define how we account for queue and run times, compute consumption, license constraints, tool utilization, storage costs, and human engineering effort. This accounting procedure remains unfinished, and we must lock down the specific tool returns that will supply each cost metric. |
| **Stopping** | We will aggressively stop any simulation attempt the moment its queue-wait or run-time deadline expires. We will halt the entire study when we resolve the intended architectural decision, exhaust all eligible capacities, consume our cycle-level budget, breach the absolute project deadline, lack a required input or tool, or discover that no alternative meets our stringent SRAM physical limits. Currently, the numeric queue-wait, run-time, and absolute deadlines remain unresolved pre-execution tasks that actively block our dispatch. |
| **Decision** | Our baseline direction rule requires an uncertainty-qualified frame-time improvement strictly greater than zero. Before initiating execution, we must prospectively define our statistical estimator, interval or confidence procedure, and any practical performance margins. Once we fix those criteria, we will recommend at most one capacity for subsequent RTL evaluation, and only if its required checks pass cleanly and its qualified comparison against the rerun baseline proves the declared performance improvement. |

: **Our declaration exposes exactly what blocks the cache run.** We clearly identify the intended requests, necessary returns, functional checks, call-count limits, and our ultimate decision criteria, while highlighting that our cache-policy bindings, derived-structure rules, statistical procedures, cost accounting, numeric deadlines, and the executable measurement path remain unfinished. {#tbl-cache-run-declaration tbl-colwidths="[22,78]"}

While our declaration explicitly fixes the required improvement direction, it does not mandate the specific statistical procedure for judging it. We must rigidly define our estimator, interval or confidence procedure, and any practical performance margin prior to simulation dispatch. We enforce this constraint to guarantee that our architecture team cannot retroactively choose a favorable statistical interpretation after observing the returns.

We specify all declared capacities and serialized values in mebibytes (MiB), where 1\ MiB equals $2^{20}$ bytes [@NISTBinaryPrefixes]. Throughout our study, these three capacity labels function as stable, immutable specification names. To maintain rigorous experimental hygiene, an executable request must cleanly propagate its declared MiB token and exact byte count into every dependent downstream request long before any baseline comparison begins.

We must stress that nothing in @tbl-cache-run-declaration was physically materialized or executed for this text. We have not run any functional regressions, coherence checks, tail-latency comparisons, power estimations, area sizing, access-time validations, thermal reviews, or IR-drop analyses to produce cache evidence here.

## Halting Design Loops Before Dispatch

While a missing implementation path derails our immediate execution, it hardly erases our study definition. Instead, it sharply limits what we can conclude as architects. We must first scrutinize exactly what our repository retained. Only after taking stock of these artifacts can we articulate what they actually prove about our unresolved design decision and firmly establish the prerequisites for a future simulation run. This methodical sequence is crucial, as it prevents us from mistaking a highly detailed architecture plan for a completed, silicon-proven experiment.

### Specification Audit

When we examine our cache material, we find two distinct classes of prospective evidence, yet absolutely nothing from an actual simulation run. First, our specification identities declare precisely what our study intends to compare. Second, our author-constructed teaching records simply illustrate what a successful execution trace *might* look like. Genuine executed evidence demands far more, requiring retained simulator requests, concrete outputs, execution statuses, and a verifiable lineage drawn directly from a live workload. As @tbl-cache-evidence-inventory illustrates, our repository successfully holds onto the first two classes while remaining completely void of executed cache evidence.

| **Retained item** | **Evidence class** | **What it supports** | **What remains absent** |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Lighthouse cache study, current design revision, controlled-state identities, and the three cache candidates | Specification identity | The cache question, comparator, intended controlled state, permitted capacity change, required measurements, call-count limits, stopping categories, and intended pre-RTL decision. | Bound policy parameters, capacity-derived cache structure, retained candidate artifacts, executable requests, runs, measurements, and a cache disposition. |
| Run declaration and its declared tool roles | Specification identity | The intended request translation, dispatch condition, return schema, failure handling, call-count limits, and tool responsibilities. | Numeric deadlines, a cost-accounting procedure, bound executables, wrapper and parser versions, exact inputs, host state, commands, logs, outputs, and realized cost. |
| Constructed SRAM and simulator entries plus a design-loop card that summarizes the proposed question, state, returns, checks, and decision | Author-constructed teaching fixture | Illustrative area, access-time, power, failure, return, and summary properties that a study record might retain. | Terminal and parser status, exact requests, raw artifacts, state identities, dispatch evidence, lineage, realized cost, and any measured cache result. |
| Retained cache execution package | Executed evidence | None. No such package is present. | Candidate artifacts, tool requests, raw outputs, parsed measurements, hashes, lineage, costs, qualified comparisons, and a decision record. |

: **Our repository retains a cache specification and teaching fixtures, not a cache experiment.** We must recognize that similar-looking identifiers across chapters do not convert our constructed entries into executed evidence. {#tbl-cache-evidence-inventory tbl-colwidths="[22,18,28,32]"}

While these constructed values effectively keep missing properties visible, they fall short of proving anything structural. They do not demonstrate that a request actually ran, nor do they confirm that we measured, rejected, or advanced any hardware candidate. For instance, the mere absence of a 4\ MiB cache request does not prove our dispatch check gracefully caught and rejected that configuration. Similarly, those illustrative 3\ MiB values fail to establish physical feasibility, measured performance, or compliance with our strict 3\ W power limit. Even our baseline entry fails to prove that we successfully reran the 2\ MiB baseline under matched, rigorous conditions. Ultimately, our listed capacities and tool roles remain mere components of a specification, rather than verified artifacts of a completed cache evaluation.

### Analytical Judgments

Even when we hit a wall before execution, we must clearly and separately report what happened to our architecture decision, the methodological contribution, the proposed mechanism, and exactly why the study stopped. Throughout this lecture, we offer the four judgments detailed in @tbl-cache-judgments as a critical lens for navigating modern computer architecture literature. Deliberately decoupling our architecture outcome from the underlying AI contribution, the hardware mechanism, and our stopping conditions exposes (rather than actively prevents) the dangerous conflation between a flashy tool demonstration and a rigorous silicon result. Note that this framework does not replace our comprehensive evaluation map in @sec-evaluating-agentic-architect, which remains essential for comparing entire agentic workflows across various hardware tasks, costs, and operating conditions.

| **Judgment** | **Cache conclusion** | **Evidence boundary** |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Architecture outcome** | Unresolved. No capacity advances, and none is rejected. | No retained cache candidate was executed, the baseline was not rerun, and no required comparison was qualified. |
| **AI contribution** | Not tested. | Direct evaluation with no added learned method was the declared approach. No AI-versus-conventional comparison exists. |
| **Mechanism** | Untested. | No retained miss classifications or matched frame observations test whether reduced capacity misses change 99th-percentile frame time. |
| **Stopping** | Stop before execution because the implementation, measurement, and dispatch prerequisites are unavailable. | The declared budget was not consumed. If the cache decision remains worth pursuing, a new run requires bound policy and derived cache choices, numeric deadlines, a cost-accounting procedure, candidate artifacts, tool bindings, request translation, and an executable measurement path. Deferral, cancellation, or reformulation remain legitimate. |

: **Our cache decision remains open for four distinct reasons.** We can see that missing execution leaves our architecture outcome unresolved, our explicit no-added-method choice leaves any AI contribution untested, missing empirical observations leave our hardware mechanism untested, and absent execution prerequisites firmly dictate our stopping point. {#tbl-cache-judgments tbl-colwidths="[18,34,48]"}

Ultimately, our stop firmly belongs before execution. We did not halt due to budget exhaustion, nor did we suffer a failed candidate or a stagnant "no-change" architectural result. Instead, this premature stop dictates that we cannot authorize any of our three proposed cache capacities for downstream RTL implementation.

## Executed Systolic-Array Study {#sec-executed-scale-study}

While our cache record illustrates where a prospective study must halt prior to execution, our separate systolic-array record begins with concrete measurements returned by actual design tools. However, we cannot distill these measurements into a single overall verdict. As architects, we must interpret them against our frozen research question, carefully separating the architecture outcome, the study-local AI contribution, the underlying mechanism result, and our subsequent design actions.

### Freezing Candidates

We retain our systolic-array study in the [tagged v0.1.7 package](https://github.com/harvard-edge/arch2/tree/f5516e52e66243c2d753191e350a5cfac56c83af/labs/examples/ai_systolic_array_study) under the name `arch2_scale_ai_study_v1`. This package rigorously preserves our preregistration, model and execution provenance, simulation results, and manifest. Preregistering the experiment fixes our architectural question, baseline comparison, and interpretation rules before our design tools return any results, ensuring that an unexpected outcome cannot retroactively alter the test methodology [@NosekEtAl2018Preregistration]. We therefore freeze our legal array shapes, scoring metric, simulation budget, rejection checks, mechanism contrast, and decision boundaries well before execution begins.

Our study evaluates systolic-array geometries across three synthetic general matrix multiplication (GEMM) layers. As is standard in accelerator design, a GEMM operation multiplies an $M \times K$ activation matrix by a $K \times N$ weight matrix to yield an $M \times N$ output matrix. We record three distinct $(M, N, K)$ dimension tuples of 128 by 128 by 256, 64 by 192 by 128, and 32 by 128 by 192. Our explicit architectural purpose here is to compare various systolic-array dimensions under a single, fixed workload and simulator configuration. Consequently, we treat these layers as isolated matrix multiplications rather than complete execution traces drawn from an identified spatial-tracking pipeline or a full XR application.

For this NPU accelerator evaluation, we employ SCALE-Sim, a cycle-accurate simulator purpose-built for systolic accelerator architectures [@RajEtAl2025ScaleSimV3]. While SCALE-Sim models internal processing element (PE) array mechanics, line buffers, and SRAM traffic under a weight-stationary dataflow, full-system evaluation of NPU accelerators often couples such spatial engines with off-chip DRAM memory models like Ramulator, a fast cycle-accurate DRAM simulator, to capture memory channel contention, row-buffer hits, and bank interleaving under heavy memory wall constraints. In our execution setup, we systematically vary array height and width in SCALE-Sim 3.0.0, holding our architecture to a weight-stationary dataflow, a fixed 128\ KiB capacity for each of the three on-chip SRAMs, and configured interface bandwidth values of 64. Our execution pipeline dispatches SCALE-Sim via Python wrapper scripts (`run_scalesim.py`), ingesting CSV workload files that define matrix dimensions for each GEMM layer and outputting structured performance summaries alongside DRAM bandwidth trace logs (`BANDWIDTH_REPORT.csv`). We derive these specific design choices directly from the package's [frozen preregistration](https://github.com/harvard-edge/arch2/blob/f5516e52e66243c2d753191e350a5cfac56c83af/labs/examples/ai_systolic_array_study/context/pre_registration.yaml) and our retained per-run configurations, rather than relying on default parameters from the original simulator paper.

Selecting weight-stationary execution ensures that weight tiles remain stationary at the processing elements while activation values stream through the array and partial sums accumulate, fundamentally reducing expensive, repeated weight data movement [@RajEtAl2025ScaleSimV3]. Our retained study deliberately enforces a strict 1,024-processing-element hardware limit, a rigid 90,000-cycle performance cutoff, and a mandatory 32 by 32 baseline. We allocate exactly four simulator evaluation events per proposal arm, alongside four shared mechanism-probe events. Although we record an 800\ MHz clock frequency to support optional derived latency calculations, we base every architectural judgment in this section strictly on cycle counts rather than wall-clock time.

We establish a fixed heuristic to serve as the budget-matched method comparator for our frozen study.

Our local, lower-is-better architectural score is

$$
S = \frac{\text{total cycles}}
         {\text{average layer utilization}/100}.
$$

Our evaluation runner computes this score directly from the retained SCALE-Sim simulation outputs. We emphasize that this score operates as a study-specific proxy; it is not a direct physical measurement, a classical area-delay product, or a universal accelerator metric. The runner calculates total cycles by summing the `Total Cycles` column, intentionally excluding the separate prefetch-inclusive column. To determine average layer utilization, we compute the arithmetic mean of the three per-layer SCALE-Sim `Overall Util %` values (rather than the `Compute Util %`), ensuring that each workload layer carries equal weight in our analysis. Consequently, our score does not explicitly penalize processing-element count, physical die area, or modeled memory traffic.

Following our frozen decision rule, a lower score indicates a superior architecture. We determine that a legal nonbaseline candidate clears our rigorous 1 percent support margin when $S_{\text{candidate}} \leq 0.99 \times S_{32\times32}$; achieving exact equality at this threshold constitutes a passing result.

Our runner constructs both evaluation arms from the identical three-row CSV workload, tracking a layer name alongside the M, N, and K dimensions for each dense GEMM. We restrict our systolic-array rows and columns strictly to the set of 8, 16, 32, 64, and 128, mandating that their product never exceed our 1,024 processing-element budget. After inserting the mandatory 32 by 32 baseline, our runner rigorously holds the workload, layout, SCALE-Sim configuration, dataflow, SRAM capacities, bandwidth parameters, performance deadlines, legality checks, and local score fixed for every candidate architecture.

We constrain our AI model's role to be equally narrow. It is permitted to return three unique, legal nonbaseline shapes and a supporting mechanism hypothesis. However, we do not allow it to invoke SCALE-Sim, waive any hardware checks, formulate the final recommendation, or autonomously make the architecture decision. Conversely, our deterministic heuristic filters out the baseline and orders every legal systolic shape first by decreasing processing-element count, then by the absolute log2 distance between the candidate's columns-to-rows ratio and the aggregate workload N-to-M ratio, and finally by increasing row and column counts. We then programmatically select the first three shapes from this sorted order. Inserting the baseline guarantees that each proposal arm receives exactly four simulator events.

### Execution Chronology

While our frozen comparison methodology dictates what the tools are allowed to evaluate, our retained chronology documents what we actually executed. We observe one initial setup failure, which precedes a valid model call and twelve successful simulator evaluation records. As @fig-array-study-workflow illustrates, a schema validation failure forces a return to the repair and revalidation phase before any proposed candidate architecture reaches the simulation stage. Structuring the workflow this way empowers our resulting record to support four separate analytical judgments, actively preventing us from conflating a raw simulator return with a reasoned architecture decision.

![**One retained record supports four separate judgments.** Our array study freezes its core question, legal design space, architectural score, budget, and hardware checks before we begin proposal selection. A schema failure immediately returns the process to repair and revalidation prior to execution. We then use the interpreted record to support distinct judgments concerning the architecture outcome, our study-local AI contribution, the proposed underlying mechanism, and the definitive stopping point.](images/ch8_design_loop_workflow){#fig-array-study-workflow width="100%" fig-alt="An architecture workflow freezes a plan and validates a proposal schema before selecting candidates, checking legality, and executing simulator runs. A failed schema returns through repair and revalidation. One shared stem from the interpreted record then branches to four boxes for the architecture outcome, study-local AI contribution, mechanism status, and stopping judgment."}

: **Our array chronology records what happened and what is missing.** Our [preregistration](https://github.com/harvard-edge/arch2/blob/f5516e52e66243c2d753191e350a5cfac56c83af/labs/examples/ai_systolic_array_study/context/pre_registration.yaml), [model provenance](https://github.com/harvard-edge/arch2/blob/f5516e52e66243c2d753191e350a5cfac56c83af/labs/examples/ai_systolic_array_study/recorded/model/provenance.json), [execution provenance](https://github.com/harvard-edge/arch2/blob/f5516e52e66243c2d753191e350a5cfac56c83af/labs/examples/ai_systolic_array_study/recorded/reference/execution_provenance.json), and [study results](https://github.com/harvard-edge/arch2/blob/f5516e52e66243c2d753191e350a5cfac56c83af/labs/examples/ai_systolic_array_study/recorded/reference/study_results.json) collectively document one schema setup failure before a valid model call, twelve completed simulator events, and no authorized acceptance or rejection. {#tbl-array-chronology tbl-colwidths="[20,40,40]"}

Because the response-format service rejects our schema prior to model inference, our record treats this failure as a routine issue in request translation and interface validation. Throughout this process, our core architecture question, legal shape set, hardware score, and evaluation budget remain entirely unchanged. We consequently treat the amendment as a necessary request repair within the boundaries of the study. However, because we lack the original schema body and the explicit service response, we cannot definitively confirm that our amendment perfectly preserved the request's intended architectural meaning.

Our [model provenance](https://github.com/harvard-edge/arch2/blob/f5516e52e66243c2d753191e350a5cfac56c83af/labs/examples/ai_systolic_array_study/recorded/model/provenance.json) records the invocation parameters, token counts, and interface metadata, but the provider omits the final currency cost and exact serving state.[^fn-model-provenance-c08] Because we lack access to the exact hosted model revision and sampling parameters, we cannot treat subsequent API calls as strict architectural reproductions of this run.

[^fn-model-provenance-c08]: **Model and interface metadata**: The execution accessed OpenAI via Codex CLI 0.144.4 (requested alias `gpt-5.4`), consuming 13,223 input tokens (1,920 cached) and 1,446 output tokens (516 reasoning tokens). The record lacks seed, temperature, top-p, and serving state parameters.

Our retained prompt suffers from a second significant provenance break. While our preregistration specifies a target prompt hash, the surviving prompt copy produces a different cryptographic hash.[^fn-prompt-hash-c08] Even though the complete model response survives in our logs, we cannot cryptographically verify the exact context that generated this architectural proposal.

[^fn-prompt-hash-c08]: **Prompt hash discrepancy**: Preregistration records SHA-256 hash `ec12df200a134532...76fbca`, whereas the surviving prompt file hashes to `36e0167aa338c6b...6971`.

Our simulator provenance records the underlying software execution stack, but it fails to bind the evaluation runner to a precise repository commit, dependency lock, container image, or host environment.[^fn-environment-provenance-c08] We acknowledge that our reference manifest exclusively covers the retained reference-output tree. It does not seal the preregistration, prompt, model response, runner source, dependency lock, and repository commit into a single, verifiable identity.

While this historical context does not inherently diagnose an error within our retained run, it explains our inability to pinpoint which missing identity, if any, might have surreptitiously altered the final execution result.

Within our retained array directory, we unfortunately lack any independently preserved validation receipt artifact. Without this crucial verification, an external architectural reviewer cannot definitively treat our reference integrity, execution replay, or focused hardware tests as independently verified. Although our retained files and the current replay pathways remain fully inspectable, any subsequent replay inherently inherits the identical workload, simulation runner, scoring mechanism, and architectural assumptions of our originally recorded computation. Crucially, our executed record lacks any study-local independent analytical models, register-transfer level (RTL) validation, or cross-simulator checks to anchor our software modeling against cycle-exact FPGA RTL behavior [@KarandikarEtAl2018FireSim]. ### Local Simulator Outputs

Our model evaluation arm assesses the mandatory 32 by 32 baseline alongside its three generated architectural proposals. Simultaneously, our fixed aggregate-aspect-ratio heuristic arm evaluates the identical baseline along with the 16 by 64, 8 by 128, and 64 by 16 array shapes. Noticeably, our two evaluation arms overlap on two distinct nonbaseline geometries. Including the repeated baseline ensures that both arms receive precisely four simulator evaluation events. As demonstrated by ArchGym (an open-source machine learning framework for architecture search), matching sample budgets proves highly effective when we compare competing architecture-search techniques [@KrishnanEtAl2023ArchGym]. In our retained study, however, we must recognize that this matched unit only equates the raw number of simulator events; it fundamentally fails to equalize the total simulator compute, model inference overhead, human setup time, heuristic construction complexity, prompt engineering effort, workflow failure penalties, rigorous review effort, or overall design cost.

Under these meticulously equalized simulator-event budgets, we observe a tied best evaluated score across both proposal arms. We treat repeated rows as discrete budget consumption events rather than statistically independent hardware measurements (@tbl-array-results).

This architectural tie demonstrates absolutely no study-local AI advantage over our deterministic, fixed heuristic when we strictly enforce equal simulator-event budgets. Furthermore, we must not mistake this tie for concrete evidence of equal capability, identical total design cost, or performance parity with rigorous exhaustive enumeration, an intensive expert study, specialized ILP solvers, or alternative hardware search methodologies. We emphasize that executing just one single proposal call supplies no statistically valid estimate of variation or broader reliability for this specific generative model family.

While our retained simulation results successfully establish that the 32 by 32 and 16 by 64 arrays yield strictly equal cycle counts and average layer utilization under our frozen scoring criteria, they completely fail to illuminate the underlying architectural root cause of that equality. Consequently, we introduce the subsequent transposition probe to rigorously test an entirely separate mechanistic hypothesis by directly contrasting the 16 by 64 array against its 64 by 16 transpose.

### Failed Directional Explanation

Our AI model confidently predicted that the 16 by 64 geometry would comfortably outperform the 64 by 16 design on our original GEMM workload, and conversely, that the 64 by 16 would dominate once we systematically exchanged the M and N matrix dimensions. However, our [retained study results](https://github.com/harvard-edge/arch2/blob/f5516e52e66243c2d753191e350a5cfac56c83af/labs/examples/ai_systolic_array_study/recorded/reference/study_results.json) report original local scores of 33,782.40 versus 54,985.25, alongside transposed scores of 23,530.65 versus 25,458.11. The model's predicted architectural reversal definitively does not occur. We conclude that simply observing a narrower performance gap under transposition does nothing to salvage the model's flawed mechanistic explanation.

Furthermore, our surviving prompt copy fatally omits the critical dataflow mapping semantics fundamentally necessary to interpret this hardware contrast. While our retained execution logs clearly identify SCALE-Sim 3.0.0, they omit any rigid dependency hash or source commit tracking. Consequently, our assumption of a K-height, N-width, and M-temporal mapping directly follows the publicly tagged v3.0.0 implementation [@ScaleSimProject2025V300Source]. Under SCALE-Sim's strict weight-stationary GEMM mode, the K dimension maps spatially across the array height and the N dimension maps across its width, while the M dimension advances temporally rather than occupying physical die area (@fig-array-mapping). In this context, a fold count represents the explicit number of array-sized passes required to tile across a mapped workload dimension, calculated as $\lceil K/\text{height}\rceil$ or $\lceil N/\text{width}\rceil$. Exchanging M and N unavoidably alters both the execution's temporal extent and its width-mapped spatial dimension, all while leaving the K dimension completely untouched. Thus, mirroring our 16 by 64 and 64 by 16 arrays simultaneously mutates both the N-fold count on the array's width and the K-fold count on its height. This means our probe entirely fails to isolate the impact of array orientation.

![**Our retained contrast ultimately fails to isolate array orientation.** Based on the tagged SCALE-Sim v3.0.0 implementation [@ScaleSimProject2025V300Source], our weight-stationary GEMM actively maps the K dimension to the physical array height and the N dimension to the array width, while the M dimension streams temporally through the processing elements. Because exchanging M and N leaves K entirely unchanged, evaluating our mirrored array shapes fundamentally alters more than just one spatial fold count at a time.](images/F8-array-mapping){#fig-array-mapping fig-alt="A GEMM workload feeds a resident weight tile of K by N, which maps onto wide 16 by 64 and tall 64 by 16 arrays. K maps over array height and N over array width. A dashed transpose connector notes that K is unchanged, so the mirrored pair changes more than one fold count."}

While our model's directional prediction thoroughly fails its publicly declared test, this botched contrast unfortunately does not establish a viable replacement mechanism. It certainly does not prove that systolic array orientation is structurally irrelevant to overall performance. Instead, we recognize that launching a robust new mechanism study would require crafting a specialized prompt with explicitly pinned mapping semantics, alongside a rigorous contrast methodology that carefully isolates and varies exactly one relevant fold count at a time.

Digging deeper, our retained report abruptly exposes a fundamental limit regarding our simulator's internal memory semantics. Specifically, the transposed 16 by 64 input configuration explicitly declares its parameters as `Bandwidth = 64,64,64`. Paradoxically, the corresponding [retained bandwidth report](https://github.com/harvard-edge/arch2/blob/f5516e52e66243c2d753191e350a5cfac56c83af/labs/examples/ai_systolic_array_study/recorded/reference/runs/probe_transposed_16x64/scalesim-results/probe_transposed_16x64/BANDWIDTH_REPORT.csv) outputs an `Avg OFMAP DRAM BW` of precisely 79.073 in one of its rows. Our historical record completely fails to explain the scaling relationship between these disjoint parameters. Because their underlying bandwidth semantics remain dangerously unresolved, we cannot treat the configured bandwidth value as valid evidence of any demonstrated physical or shared-system bottleneck.

This static word-counting abstraction in SCALE-Sim stands in stark contrast to cycle-accurate memory subsystem simulators like Ramulator 2.0 or gem5's memory controllers [@KimEtAl2015Ramulator; @LuoEtAl2024Ramulator2]. While SCALE-Sim assumes an ideal memory interface where DRAM throughput scales linearly with requested word count, Ramulator models the explicit microarchitecture of modern DRAM systems, including memory channels, ranks, bank groups, individual banks, and row buffers. When we evaluate real-world DRAM controllers, we must account for strict physical timing constraints ($t_{\mathrm{RCD}}$ row-to-column delay, $t_{\mathrm{RAS}}$ row access strobe time, $t_{\mathrm{RP}}$ row precharge time, and $t_{\mathrm{CAS}}$ column access strobe latency), write-to-read bus turnaround delays ($t_{\mathrm{WTR}}$), and periodic refresh stalls ($t_{\mathrm{RFC}}$).

When we evaluate an accelerator design using cycle-accurate DRAM modeling, memory latency is governed by bank conflict rates and row buffer hit ratios rather than raw transfer volumes. When we model our accelerator under open-page memory controller policies, consecutive requests from our array to the same DRAM row hit the row buffer instantly with minimum latency ($t_{\mathrm{CAS}}$). However, if our NPU array shape alters the memory access stride, such as streaming matrix columns from non-contiguous memory addresses, our requests hit different rows within the same bank. This forces our memory controller to issue a precharge command ($t_{\mathrm{RP}}$) followed by an activate command ($t_{\mathrm{RCD}}$) before reading data, incurring a severe row buffer miss penalty.

For instance, while SCALE-Sim reports that our 16 by 64 array requires 409,726 DRAM word writes compared to 204,863 for the 32 by 32 baseline, it treats all 409,726 writes as uniform, unconstrained accesses. Under a cycle-accurate Ramulator simulation, if the 16 by 64 geometry's wide spatial layout causes strided memory accesses that cross bank boundaries out of order, bank conflicts and row-buffer thrashing can double or triple our effective memory stall cycles. Conversely, if a narrower array alignment allows our memory controller to execute row-buffer-consecutive burst transfers, our DRAM channel utilization increases dramatically. Evaluating memory subsystems at full depth requires us to capture these command queue delays, arbiter policies, and physical bank interactions rather than relying solely on high-level word-counting abstractions.

Taking a step back, we must concede that our retained SCALE-Sim configuration and corresponding outputs successfully establish virtually none of the 8 prompt stack layers required by our overarching Lighthouse system decision. This specific execution run preserves no usable data concerning RV64GCV vector ISA compliance, Triton JIT to RVV 1.0 lowering correctness, Ramulator DRAM timing delays, TSMC N7 physical layout constraints, dynamic energy, peak power, die area, Ansys RedHawk-SC thermal dissipation, UPF IEEE 1801 power domain isolation, or SystemVerilog Assertion (SVA) formal proofs. This omission is particularly glaring given that the broader SCALE-Sim v3 framework actively supports detailed memory and energy analyses [@RajEtAl2025ScaleSimV3]. Furthermore, our arbitrarily configured bandwidth parameters and the simulator's reported operand traffic completely fail to model a verified, contention-aware shared-system interface. In the end, this synthetic GEMM workload and our highly localized array result cannot definitively resolve the system-level cache sizing decision for XRBench, SPEC2026, or MLPerf Mobile workloads, satisfy our rigid 3\ W TDP thermal envelope, or successfully close out the Lighthouse accelerator design.

When we examine our executed results, we find them surprisingly narrow, even for this tightly scoped local array question. We are working within a small, closed legal design space containing exactly fifteen architectural shapes, constrained by our declared dimensions and a strict 1,024-processing-element limit. Yet, our retained proposal-arm evaluations explore only five of these fifteen legal shapes. This leaves ten potential array configurations completely uncharacterized and without any executed simulation result (@tbl-array-shape-coverage).

| Not executed | 8 by 8; 8 by 16; 8 by 32; 8 by 64; 16 by 8; 16 by 16; 16 by 32; 32 by 8; 64 by 8; 128 by 8 | 10 |

: **Five evaluated geometries do not close our fifteen-shape architectural space.** While our repeated arm events faithfully preserve our frozen budgets, they contribute no new geometrical insights. Consequently, we are left without any retained SCALE-Sim results for the ten remaining legal shapes. {#tbl-array-shape-coverage tbl-colwidths="[25,62,13]"}

If we intend to freeze a follow-up study, we could achieve a comprehensive full-space reference through exhaustive enumeration (evaluating every single legal shape under a fixed workload, simulator configuration, scoring metric, and set of checks). However, we must recognize that such a brute-force approach does not match the computation budget of our current four-event proposal arms. In our next architectural iteration, we must explicitly budget for this greater simulation cost or strictly use it as a foundational coverage baseline. Since we did not perform that enumeration in our current study, we cannot confidently infer any performance outcomes for the ten unexecuted shapes. Furthermore, we cannot retroactively simulate these missing shapes just to claim our recorded model tied or outperformed the complete architectural design space.

Our frozen score also critically omits a reported performance axis that could deeply influence our future system-level decisions. For instance, the 16 by 64 shape ties our baseline performance at exactly 13,917 cycles and 41.196 percent average layer utilization. Yet, when we dig into our [retained study results](https://github.com/harvard-edge/arch2/blob/f5516e52e66243c2d753191e350a5cfac56c83af/labs/examples/ai_systolic_array_study/recorded/reference/study_results.json), we discover 409,726 modeled DRAM writes for the 16 by 64 geometry compared to just 204,863 for our 32 by 32 baseline. In another stark contrast, our 64 by 16 shape reports 102,400 modeled writes and fewer total modeled accesses than the baseline, despite taking far more cycles to execute. We must remember that these numbers represent abstract simulator outputs, rather than true physical DRAM transactions or concrete energy measurements.

When we evaluate the two reported metrics of cycles and modeled writes together, our baseline clearly dominates the shared 16 by 64 candidate (@fig-proxy-mismatch). This important post-run observation exposes a fundamental limitation in the proxies we used to model our architecture. However, we cannot let this insight retroactively alter our frozen score, nor does it establish actual physical memory energy consumption or authorize us to change our prior design decision.

## Technical Boundaries of Architectural Loop Execution


::: {.callout-design-principle title="Seminal Principle. Prospective vs Executed Rigor"}
Architectural intent requires absolute separation from executed proof. Prospective specifications frame valid search spaces for host CPU and NPU spatial array geometries. Only concrete executed runs (e.g., SCALE-Sim, Ramulator, gem5) instantiate silicon-plausible evidence. Conflating unexecuted plans with physically modeled outcomes destroys empirical validity.
:::

When we evaluate the Lighthouse cache path alongside our separate executed array study, we see that they hit entirely different technical stopping points. Naturally, they also drive different architectural next steps (@tbl-lighthouse-return).

Looking closely at the executed array case, we find that every returned signal forces us to rethink a different architectural claim and pivot our subsequent actions. We can handle some of these actions within our current record, but others demand that we freeze a completely new architectural study.

- **Tie:** When our returned scores challenge the claim that model-guided proposals improve local architecture outcomes, we must adjust our expectations. Because these proposals demonstrate no study-local advantage over our fixed heuristic under equal simulator-event budgets, we simply retain 32 by 32 for our evaluated set. If we want to claim broader selection benefits, we must run a newly frozen, separately budgeted full-space reference.
- **Failed mechanism:** Our transposition results alter our directional explanation rather than our measured ranking. They squarely reject our predicted reversal, yet they fail to offer a replacement mechanism. To isolate what is actually happening in the hardware, we need a newly frozen study built on pinned mapping semantics.
- **Omitted metric:** Once we look at our modeled traffic counts, we expose a critical quantity absent from the frozen score. These counts neither change our current ranking nor allow us to perform post-run rescoring. Instead, they remind us that if we rely on a memory-aware decision quantity, we must build it into a newly frozen study.
- **Provenance gap:** Because we lack prompt identity and full simulator provenance, we cannot make a strong claim for architectural reproduction. While we can still use our current record within these constraints, any new run must rigorously capture the exact prompt, model revision (when available), runner revision, dependencies, command sequences, and complete outputs.
- **Pending authority:** Although our machine-readable technical recommendation retains 32 by 32 for the evaluated set, we have not recorded any authorized acceptance or rejection. Therefore, our immediate next action within the current record must be a peer review rather than a firm architectural commitment.

Our tie, our failed mechanism, our omitted metric, and our provenance gap all point toward necessary follow-up studies. We did not run any of these as part of our retained execution, and each will require its own separately frozen architectural comparison. Even if we completed those studies, we still would not fully establish XR behavior or hit our 3\ W system target, simply because our retained configurations and outputs lack the necessary system-level checks.

| Lighthouse cache path | Unresolved. We neither evaluated, rejected, nor advanced any cache candidate. | Not tested. We selected direct evaluation without any added learned methods. | Untested. We retained no result connecting capacity misses to 99th-percentile frame time. | Stop before execution. We lack the cache implementation, measurement, and dispatch prerequisites. If we believe this decision remains worth pursuing, we must launch a new fully retained run that supplies all missing bindings, procedures, and artifacts. Otherwise, we can legitimately defer, cancel, or reformulate. |
| Separate executed array study | No evaluated nonbaseline design clears our local margin across five unique shapes. We do not claim this as an optimality result. | We demonstrate no study-local advantage over the fixed heuristic under equal simulator-event budgets. We also failed to measure equal total cost and method parity. | Our directional reversal prediction fails, and we establish no replacement explanation. | Our machine-readable recommendation retains 32 by 32 for the evaluated set, stopping our local technical search. We recorded no authorized acceptance or rejection. |

: **We find that our two records stop at fundamentally different technical boundaries.** Our Lighthouse cache path never reaches execution, while our separate retained array study executes only a narrow simulator comparison for which we recorded no authorized acceptance or rejection. Because these are not cohesive stages of a single end-to-end Lighthouse run, neither result can finalize the other. {#tbl-lighthouse-return tbl-colwidths="[19,22,20,18,21]"}

When we step back, both records leave our core system-level questions completely open. Neither trace explicitly identifies an XR workload, nor does either validate our tail deadlines across actual deployed conditions. Furthermore, we never execute the compiler, the runtime, the RISC-V interface, our host cores, the shared memory path, our sensors, or the display engine. When scaling across distributed multi-node compute clusters, our execution pipeline must maintain multi-node state synchronization, logging atomic rollback artifacts whenever a cluster worker encounters an unrecoverable simulator crash or host kernel preemption. Ultimately, neither record provides a complete verification plan or fully validates the function, security, or reliability of our overall subsystem.

Crucially, our physical design questions also remain unanswered. We retain no concrete evidence that closes our timing, routing, area, or power delivery constraints. We have yet to prove our 3\ W subsystem budget, characterize our thermal behavior, or verify our final silicon performance. While our array reports do include modeled local traffic, we lack a shared-memory contention analysis or a physical energy model to connect that traffic back to the Lighthouse platform. Our cache plan might name some of these essential physical checks, but simply naming a check in architecture is never a substitute for actually running it.

## Open Questions

When we examine the unexecuted Lighthouse cache plan alongside our constrained systolic array records, we hit the exact limits of how well we can currently reason through stalled workflows and incomplete evidence. We are looking at the very frontier of our automation capabilities. These gaps go far beyond simple engineering inconveniences; they pose deep methodological challenges right where our rigorous evaluation frameworks collide with the chaotic realities of tool failures, partial synthesis results, and tight execution budgets. If we want to transform our ad-hoc automation scripts into genuinely robust architectural workflows, we must solve these problems. We have to develop principled stopping rules, create dynamic methods for allocating simulation capacity, and design unbiased techniques for adapting our plans on the fly. For those of us charting the next generation of AI-assisted computer architecture, these exact friction points offer phenomenal opportunities for high-impact dissertations and pivotal publications that will fundamentally reshape how we establish trust in automated hardware design decisions.

### Budget Allocation

Whenever we launch a complex architectural study, we constantly face a critical triage of whether to push forward and execute, pause to repair a broken state, or completely reformulate our approach. And crucially, how do we best spend our severely limited evaluation capacity?

- **Action selection:** When our automated workflows inevitably slam into missing prerequisites (like those unbound cache policies we saw earlier) or stumble over interface failures such as rejected schemas, how exactly should they decide their next move? We must develop rigorous, measurable ways to evaluate different action-selection policies. We want to judge them by their total cost to reach a fully supported architectural conclusion, as well as their knack for sidestepping invalid tool dispatches and pointless reformulations.

- **Capacity allocation:** Every study forces us to ration our tight budgets for simulation, RTL implementation, and manual review across a fierce competition of design candidates and correctness checks. How do we pinpoint the optimal strategy? We need to rigorously compare fixed, cheapest-first, and decision-aware allocation policies under identical budgets. We must observe how frequently they successfully resolve our core architectural questions, quantify the compute cycles they squander after a decision is already clear, and track how often they overlook a dark-horse candidate that might have completely flipped our final conclusion.

### Stopping Rules

As our evaluations run, inevitable failures and early interim results will often justify pivoting our plan. However, we have to ensure that these mid-flight adjustments never retroactively skew our baseline comparisons or artificially inflate the confidence of our latest supported result.

We often see our machine learning colleagues leverage techniques like Hyperband, an adaptive resource allocation algorithm for hyperparameter optimization [@LiEtAl2018Hyperband] to aggressively cull weak configurations based on early, low-fidelity signals. But computer architecture evaluation is an entirely different domain. In our work, we routinely deal with monolithic RTL simulations, exhaustive formal-verification sweeps, synthesis jobs, and physical-design runs that are strictly indivisible. They rarely offer a trustworthy intermediate fidelity, and we simply cannot discard them mid-run without obliterating the coverage we require. So, while Hyperband gives us a brilliant conceptual spark for resource allocation, it hardly proves that aggressive adaptive stopping can cleanly map onto our architectural toolchains.

- **Revising experiments:** At what precise point does adapting our experimental plan to fresh data blur into dangerous outcome bias? We have to establish robust methodologies to weigh the tradeoffs here. We need to know the difference between intelligently steering our subsequent simulation runs toward the most promising design space, versus compromising the fundamental validity of our comparative baseline. We must quantify this delicate balance by analyzing candidate coverage and the ultimate quality of our supported decisions under strictly matched tool budgets.

- **Stopping rules:** What actually makes a stopping rule mathematically sound in an architectural context? A truly robust rule has to protect us from two extremes. It must stop us from burning precious compute cycles once the core architectural decision is definitively settled, while simultaneously blocking us from making premature claims based on half-baked evidence, as demonstrated by our systolic array study's abrupt technical stop. We must rigorously measure our decision quality, the bloat in our tool and review costs, the frequency of premature halts, and any unsupported conclusions against a standard fixed-budget policy.

## Common Architectural Pitfalls

When we execute iterative design loops without strict evidence boundaries, we severely undermine our architectural decision-making. As we orchestrate automated evaluation pipelines across complex simulation, synthesis, and physical layout stages, we frequently stumble into critical traps regarding prospective parameter binding, evidence retention, and adaptive stopping.

- **Conflating prospective plans with executed evidence:** When we treat prospective trial specifications, generator prompts, or configuration scripts as if they were verified execution records, we confuse setup intent with empirical proof. Generating elaborate evaluation plans and candidate configurations merely establishes setup intent. Until our simulation binaries, gate-level netlists, or formal proofs execute and emit verified physical artifacts, our candidate architecture remains entirely unmeasured.

- **Violating prospective binding rules through retrospective tuning:** When we adjust evaluation parameters, simulation seeds, workload trace windows, or EDA tool constraints after observing interim candidate scores, we violate prospective binding rules. These rules require us to lock experimental parameters prior to execution. Modifying evaluation conditions mid-loop to favor specific candidates introduces severe outcome bias and destroys the comparative integrity of our baseline study.[^fn-fda-preregistration-c08]

[^fn-fda-preregistration-c08]: **Clinical trial preregistration parallel**: In biomedical research, FDA regulatory frameworks require protocols, primary endpoints, and statistical analysis plans to be registered prior to trial initiation to prevent post-hoc data dredging and outcome switching [@NosekEtAl2018Preregistration]. In computer architecture, locking trace windows, workload seeds, and EDA synthesis constraints prior to execution plays an identical role, preserving baseline comparative integrity.

- **Substituting retained metadata for executed verification evidence:** When we rely on cached trial metadata, historical run logs, or partial pipeline outputs from disjoint studies to justify new design decisions, we bypass actual execution. While retaining metadata across design loops accelerates our study lineage tracking, cached logs from older toolchains or altered operating conditions cannot substitute for executed signoff checks on our current candidate design.

- **Misinterpreting budget-limited ties as architectural equivalence:** When we conflate equal candidate scores under tightly constrained simulation budgets with physical hardware parity, we misread the return. When our automated search heuristic ties with a baseline architecture under a restricted cycle-budget, the result indicates that our allocated compute was insufficient to resolve a performance delta, rather than proving equivalent hardware capability.[^fn-optimizers-curse-c08]

[^fn-optimizers-curse-c08]: **Decision analysis parallel**: In decision theory, selecting candidates based on budget-constrained or surrogate evaluations introduces the *optimizer's curse* [@SmithWinkler2006OptimizersCurse], where selected candidates preferentially capture optimistic estimation errors. A budget-limited tie reflects evaluation truncation rather than true hardware parity, requiring higher-fidelity signoff before declaring equivalence.

- **Coupling microarchitectural mechanisms with unverified system outcomes:** When we attribute a candidate's high-level score improvement to a hypothesized microarchitectural mechanism without executing isolating diagnostic checks, we risk false causal claims. Candidate hardware often outperforms a baseline due to secondary effects like altered compiler code alignment or cache line prefetching shifts. We must decouple the true cause from the aggregate score to protect our architectural conclusions.

## Conclusion

::: {.callout-design-principle title="Claim only what the checked record supports"}
The verified execution record forms a rigid upper bound on our architectural
claims. A prospective plan, an executed artifact, a local simulation result, and a stopping
condition remain distinctly separated in our methodology. We cannot simply substitute data from an
unexecuted plan or a disjoint local study to gloss over an evidence gap in our design. Every claim
we make must trace directly back to retained execution artifacts and strictly validated checks. When our
research question changes, we must freeze a new study's state; any previous evidence
remains confined to its original architectural scope.
:::

When we evaluate the Lighthouse cache study, we see that it reaches a supported stop before architectural execution even begins. Our methodology fails to retain critical policy bindings, capacity-derived structures, numeric deadlines, and measurement pipelines, leaving our repository with zero backing for any definitive architecture recommendation.

Turning to the separate array study, we encounter a substantially different stopping point. Our execution record retains a tied local score against a fixed heuristic and a failed directional explanation, ultimately stopping with a conservative recommendation to retain the 32 by 32 array configuration. Because we recorded no authorized acceptance or rejection, our study fundamentally cannot establish array optimality or any meaningful full-system XR result.

Ultimately, neither execution record yields a definitive "win" claim for our designs. If we pursue the cache decision, our next execution must rigorously integrate those missing procedures and measurement paths. Likewise, if we want to make a broader array candidate-selection claim, we must deploy a newly frozen, separately budgeted full-space comparison followed by the rigorous system-relevant checks that were absent from our initially retained run.
